items.definition: Vague and unclear, with no clear shape or details.
items.explanation: From Latin nebula, 'cloud'. It is often used for ideas, plans, or memories.
items.example: Her plans for the future were still nebulous, with no dates or details.
items.picture_idea: A hazy cloud of mist hiding the outline of a shape
items.definition_previous: vague, unclear, or not well defined

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: lacking definition or definite content

items.definition: Very wicked, especially in a way that is meant to cause harm.
items.example: The detective uncovered the villain's nefarious scheme to steal the museum's treasures.
items.picture_idea: A shadowy figure in a cloak sneaking through a dark room
items.definition_previous: wicked or criminal

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: extremely wicked

items.definition: Calm and relaxed, showing no worry or interest in something that others might care about.
items.explanation: Comes from French. It can describe someone who seems casual even in an exciting or tense moment.
items.example: He gave a nonchalant shrug when they announced he had won.
items.picture_idea: A person shrugging with a relaxed smile
items.definition_previous: calm and relaxed, as if not worried or interested

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: marked by blithe unconcern

items.definition: A very small difference in meaning, feeling, or tone that is hard to notice.
items.example: A good translator must understand the nuances of both languages.
items.picture_idea: Two nearly identical shades of blue side by side
items.definition_previous: a small, subtle difference in meaning, tone, or color

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: a subtle difference in meaning or opinion or attitude

items.definition: To make something hard to understand or unclear, often on purpose.
items.explanation: Often used when someone confuses a topic on purpose, such as with complicated wording.
items.example: The company tried to obfuscate the problem with long, technical reports.
items.picture_idea: A person hiding a page of text behind swirling smoke
items.definition_previous: to make something unclear or hard to understand

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: make obscure or unclear

items.definition: Meant to catch people's attention and impress them, often by showing off money or things.
items.example: The millionaire's ostentatious mansion had gold fountains on the lawn.
items.picture_idea: A huge mansion with gold fountains and a fancy car
items.definition_previous: showy in a way meant to impress others

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: intended to attract notice and impress others

items.definition: Giving a sign that something bad may soon happen.
items.example: Dark, ominous clouds gathered above the picnic.
items.picture_idea: Black storm clouds rolling over an empty field
items.definition_previous: suggesting that something bad is about to happen

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: threatening or foreshadowing evil or tragic developments

items.definition: A widely accepted way of thinking about a subject; also a typical example or model.
items.explanation: In science, a 'paradigm shift' is a big change in how people understand a subject.
items.example: The discovery of germs caused a paradigm shift in medicine.
items.definition_previous: a typical model or pattern; a way of thinking about something

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: the generally accepted perspective of a particular discipline at a given time

items.definition: Harmful in a slow, hidden way that is hard to notice or stop.
items.example: Rumors can have a pernicious effect on a friendship.
items.picture_idea: A weed slowly strangling a healthy plant
items.definition_previous: harmful in a slow, hidden way

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: working or spreading in a hidden and usually injurious way

items.definition: The fresh, earthy smell in the air when rain first falls on dry ground.
items.explanation: The word was coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists, from Greek petra 'stone' and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods.
items.example: We opened the windows to enjoy the petrichor after the first storm of summer.
items.picture_idea: Raindrops hitting dry, dusty earth
items.definition_previous: the pleasant smell of rain falling on dry ground

definition_basis.note: WordNet has no entry for this word; written by Claude

items.definition: A very large amount of something, more than is needed.
items.explanation: Usually used in the phrase 'a plethora of'.
items.example: The menu offered a plethora of choices, so it took her ages to decide.
items.picture_idea: A table overflowing with many different dishes
items.definition_previous: a large amount, more than is needed

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: extreme excess

items.definition: A cure or answer that people claim will solve every problem.
items.explanation: Often used in negative sentences, such as 'there is no panacea'.
items.example: Technology is not a panacea for every problem in schools.
items.picture_idea: A magic bottle labeled 'cures everything'
items.definition_previous: a cure or solution that is said to fix all problems

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: hypothetical remedy for all ills or diseases; once sought by the alchemists

items.definition: Dealing with problems in a practical, sensible way instead of focusing on ideas or hopes.
items.example: Taking a pragmatic approach, she chose the cheaper option that still worked well.
items.picture_idea: A person comparing two tools and choosing the useful one
items.definition_previous: dealing with things in a practical, sensible way

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: concerned with practical matters

items.definition: Full of high hopes and ideals that are not practical or realistic.
items.explanation: From Don Quixote, the hero of a Spanish novel who fought windmills thinking they were giants.
items.example: His quixotic plan to plant a forest in the desert amazed everyone.
items.picture_idea: A knight on a horse charging at a windmill
items.definition_previous: idealistic in a way that is not realistic or practical

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: not sensible about practical matters; idealistic and unrealistic

items.definition: A state of not knowing what to do when you face a hard choice.
items.example: She was in a quandary over which invitation to accept.
items.picture_idea: A person standing at a fork in the road scratching their head
items.definition_previous: a state of not knowing what to do in a difficult situation

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: state of uncertainty or perplexity especially as requiring a choice between equally unfavorable options

items.definition: Stubbornly refusing to obey or to do what you are told.
items.example: The recalcitrant mule would not move, no matter how hard we pulled.
items.picture_idea: A mule planting its feet while a person tugs the rope
items.definition_previous: stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: stubbornly resistant to authority or control

items.definition: Not willing to talk about your thoughts or feelings; quiet and reserved.
items.example: He was reticent about his past and rarely spoke of his childhood.
items.picture_idea: A person with a finger to their lips
items.definition_previous: unwilling to share thoughts or feelings; reserved

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: temperamentally disinclined to talk

items.definition: Able to recover quickly from trouble or hard times; also able to bounce back into shape.
items.example: Children are often more resilient than adults expect.
items.picture_idea: A bent branch springing back upright
items.definition_previous: able to recover quickly from difficulty or to spring back into shape

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: recovering readily from adversity, depression, or the like

items.definition: Good luck in finding something good by chance when you were not looking for it.
items.explanation: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 from a fairy tale, 'The Three Princes of Serendip'.
items.example: It was pure serendipity that we met on the same train.
items.picture_idea: A person happily finding a coin on the pavement
items.definition_previous: a happy accident; finding something good by chance

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: good luck in making unexpected and fortunate discoveries

items.definition: A person who praises powerful people too much in order to get something from them.
items.example: The king was surrounded by sycophants who agreed with everything he said.
items.picture_idea: A group of people bowing and clapping around a king
items.definition_previous: a person who flatters important people to gain favor

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: a person who tries to please someone in order to gain a personal advantage

items.definition: More than you need, so not necessary.
items.example: The editor cut every superfluous word from the article.
items.picture_idea: A red pen crossing out extra words on a page
items.definition_previous: more than is needed; unnecessary

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: more than is needed, desired, or required

items.definition: Staying calm and showing no feelings when facing pain or trouble.
items.explanation: From Stoicism, an ancient Greek philosophy that taught people to stay calm and accept what they cannot change.
items.example: She remained stoic as the doctor explained the long recovery.
items.picture_idea: A calm person standing in heavy rain without flinching
items.definition_previous: calm and showing no emotion when facing pain or trouble

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: seeming unaffected by pleasure or pain; impassive

items.definition: Seeming true or real, but actually false.
items.explanation: Often used for claims, arguments, or evidence that sound right but are not.
items.example: The scientist rejected the spurious claim because it had no evidence.
items.picture_idea: A magnifying glass revealing a fake signature
items.definition_previous: false or fake, though made to look real

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: ostensibly valid, but not actually valid

items.definition: Happening now and then, at scattered times, not in a regular pattern.
items.example: Sporadic showers fell throughout the afternoon.
items.picture_idea: A few scattered raindrops falling from a mostly clear sky
items.definition_previous: happening now and then, not regularly

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: recurring in scattered and irregular or unpredictable instances

items.definition: Holding firmly to a goal and refusing to give up.
items.example: The tenacious climber kept going despite the freezing wind.
items.picture_idea: A climber gripping a cliff face with determination
items.definition_previous: holding on firmly; refusing to give up

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: stubbornly unyielding

items.definition: Saying very little and not liking to talk, as part of your nature.
items.example: The old fisherman was taciturn and spoke only when necessary.
items.picture_idea: An old man sitting silently by a boat
items.definition_previous: saying very little; quiet by nature

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: habitually reserved and uncommunicative

items.definition: A nervous feeling of fear about something that is about to happen.
items.example: She opened the exam paper with trepidation.
items.picture_idea: A nervous person peeking through half-closed fingers at a door
items.definition_previous: a feeling of fear or worry about something that may happen

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: a feeling of alarm or dread

items.definition: Real and clear enough that you can see it, show it, or prove it.
items.explanation: The opposite is 'intangible'. Tangible results are results you can clearly see.
items.example: The project produced tangible results: three new classrooms.
items.picture_idea: A hand touching a solid object
items.definition_previous: able to be touched or clearly seen to be real

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: capable of being treated as fact

items.definition: Found everywhere, or seeming to be everywhere at the same time.
items.explanation: From Latin ubique, 'everywhere'.
items.example: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern life.
items.picture_idea: A crowd of people all looking at phones
items.definition_previous: seeming to be everywhere at once

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: being present everywhere at once

items.definition: Clear and firm, leaving no doubt about what is meant.
items.example: The judge gave an unequivocal answer: the rule applied to everyone.
items.picture_idea: A person firmly pointing and nodding
items.definition_previous: clear and firm, with no doubt

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: admitting of no doubt or misunderstanding; having only one meaning or interpretation and leading to only one conclusion

items.definition: To take someone's power or place unfairly, often by force, when it is not yours to take.
items.example: The prince's uncle tried to usurp the throne.
items.picture_idea: A man snatching a crown from a king's head
items.definition_previous: to take power or a position by force or without the right

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: seize and take control without authority and possibly with force; take as one's right or possession

items.definition: To respect someone or something very deeply and treat them with great honor.
items.example: Many cultures venerate their elders for their wisdom.
items.picture_idea: Young people bowing respectfully to an elderly person
items.definition_previous: to treat with great respect and honor

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: regard with feelings of respect and reverence; consider hallowed or exalted or be in awe of

items.definition: Felt by watching or hearing about other people, instead of by doing something yourself.
items.example: He got vicarious pleasure from watching his sister's travel videos.
items.picture_idea: A person at home smiling while watching a friend's trip on a screen
items.definition_previous: felt or experienced through someone else rather than yourself

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: experienced at secondhand

items.definition: A small sign or trace that is left of something that was once there.
items.example: Only a few vestiges of the ancient wall remain.
items.picture_idea: A crumbling stone fragment of an old wall in a field
items.definition_previous: a small trace of something that once existed

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: an indication that something has been present

items.definition: Likely to change suddenly, especially by becoming angry or violent.
items.explanation: Used for tempers, markets, and situations, and in chemistry for liquids that turn to gas easily.
items.example: The volatile situation could turn violent at any moment.
items.picture_idea: A bubbling flask with vapor rising quickly
items.definition_previous: likely to change suddenly or become violent; evaporating quickly

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: liable to lead to sudden change or violence

items.definition: To clear someone of blame by showing with proof that they were right or innocent.
items.example: The new evidence vindicated the accused man.
items.picture_idea: A person being declared innocent in a courtroom
items.definition_previous: to clear someone of blame or show that they were right

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: clear of accusation, blame, suspicion, or doubt with supporting proof

items.definition: To slowly become smaller, weaker, or less.
items.explanation: Used for the moon when it shows less of its face each night. The opposite is 'wax'.
items.example: Her interest in the hobby began to wane after a few months.
items.picture_idea: The moon shrinking from full to a thin crescent
items.definition_previous: to gradually become smaller, weaker, or less

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: grow smaller

items.definition: Playful and a little strange in a charming way.
items.example: The garden had whimsical statues of frogs wearing hats.
items.picture_idea: A frog statue wearing a tiny top hat in a garden
items.definition_previous: playful and unusual in a charming way

definition_basis.note: no WordNet meaning fit; written by Claude
definition_basis.batch_note: The only WordNet meaning (acting on a sudden whim, unpredictable) does not match our definition or example, which mean playful and charming.

items.definition: Quietly sad as you think about something you miss or wish you had.
items.example: He gave a wistful smile as he looked at old photographs.
items.picture_idea: A person gazing out a window holding an old photo
items.definition_previous: feeling a quiet, sad longing for something

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: showing pensive sadness

items.definition: Fear or strong dislike of people from other countries or ways of life.
items.explanation: From Greek xenos 'stranger' and phobos 'fear'.
items.example: The campaign aimed to fight xenophobia by celebrating cultural diversity.
items.definition_previous: dislike or fear of people from other countries or cultures

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: a fear of foreigners or strangers

items.definition: A wooden bar that goes across the necks of two animals so they can pull together.
items.explanation: Figuratively, 'the yoke of tyranny' means harsh control over people.
items.example: The oxen wore a heavy wooden yoke as they pulled the plow.
items.picture_idea: Two oxen joined by a wooden bar pulling a plow
items.definition_previous: a wooden bar that joins two animals so they can pull a load together; something that oppresses

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: stable gear that joins two draft animals at the neck so they can work together as a team

items.definition: The main ideas and mood of a certain time in history.
items.explanation: A German word meaning 'time spirit', borrowed into English.
items.example: The film captured the zeitgeist of the 1960s.
items.definition_previous: the spirit or mood of a particular period in history

definition_basis.note: WordNet has no entry for this word; written by Claude

items.definition: The highest point or best time of something.
items.example: The Roman Empire reached its zenith in the second century.
items.picture_idea: The sun at its highest point directly above a mountain
items.definition_previous: the highest point; the point in the sky directly overhead

definition_basis.note: no WordNet meaning fit; written by Claude
definition_basis.batch_note: WordNet only lists the astronomical sense (point in the sky overhead), which does not match our example about the highest point of something.

items.definition: Very eager and full of energy for something you strongly believe in.
items.example: The zealous volunteers cleaned the whole beach before noon.
items.picture_idea: Eager volunteers picking up litter on a beach
items.definition_previous: full of energy and strong enthusiasm for a cause

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: marked by active interest and enthusiasm

items.definition: The lowest or worst point of something.
items.explanation: The opposite of zenith. It comes from Arabic and also means the point in the sky directly below you.
items.example: Losing his job was the nadir of an awful year.
items.picture_idea: A graph line dropping to its lowest point
items.definition_previous: the lowest point of something

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: an extreme state of adversity; the lowest point of anything

items.definition: Refusing to change your mind or your way of doing things, even when others ask you to.
items.example: The obstinate child refused to wear a coat even in the snow.
items.picture_idea: A child with folded arms shaking their head
items.definition_previous: stubbornly refusing to change your mind

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: tenaciously unwilling or marked by tenacious unwillingness to yield

items.definition: So strong that you can almost feel it; very easy to notice.
items.example: The tension in the room was palpable.
items.picture_idea: People sitting stiffly in a silent, tense room
items.definition_previous: so strong that it can almost be felt; easy to notice

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: so intense as to be almost touched or felt

items.definition: Hopeful and cheerful about how things will turn out, even when things are hard.
items.explanation: From Latin sanguis, 'blood'. Medieval people believed a lot of blood made someone cheerful.
items.example: Despite the delays, she remained sanguine about the project's success.
items.picture_idea: A smiling person looking up at a sunrise
items.definition_previous: hopeful and optimistic, especially in a difficult situation

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: confidently optimistic and cheerful

items.definition: Ready to argue or fight, and rude or angry toward others.
items.example: The truculent customer shouted at everyone in the shop.
items.picture_idea: A scowling person with clenched fists
items.definition_previous: eager to argue or fight; aggressively defiant

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: defiantly aggressive

items.definition: Sweet and charming in an innocent way that makes people like them.
items.example: The little girl gave a winsome smile and won over the whole class.
items.picture_idea: A child with a bright, charming smile
items.definition_previous: charming and attractive in an innocent way

definition_basis.wordnet_meaning: charming in a childlike or naive way
